want.now.why: The door 'wott' sits second and pushes the infinitive to the end, so the object slips in between: Ich wott Khasi lerne.

want.past.why: No Präteritum: tense goes on 'ha' in second place and the door drops to the very end as 'wele' (same shape as the infinitive), after the verb.

want.neg.why: 'nöd' comes right after the door, before object and infinitive; no do-support of any kind.

want.q.why: Yes/no question by pure inversion: 'wotsch' moves to the front and is the question marker itself. Friends often drop 'du' (Wotsch Khasi lerne?).

decline.now.why: Causal glue is 'wil' (wo is only temporal/relative in Zürich). Unlike Standard German the modal stays before its infinitive: wil ich mues schaffe.

decline.past.why: Both doors go Perfekt with 'ha' plus a bare infinitive, never a participle: cho chöne, ha müese schaffe. Clause 2 keeps aux-modal-verb order after 'wil'.

decline.fut.why: No future form: 'morn' carries the whole 'won't be able to'. CAN needs no substitute, and clause 2 stays bare present after 'wil'.

decline.although.why: 'obwohl' behaves like 'wil': the second clause keeps modal-before-infinitive. Spoken Zürich often prefers 'au wänn' (even if) for the same job.

like.now.why: LIKE is 'gern haa': the door splits, 'ha' in second place carries person, 'gern' waits at the end, and the object sits inside the bracket.

like.neg.why: The negative usually switches door to 'mag' with 'nöd' at the very end (Ich ha Kafi nöd gern also works but is less common in Zürich).

like.she.why: Only the first half of the split door changes for third person: ha becomes hät; 'gern' never inflects.

like.q.why: Inversion again: the inflected half 'häsch' fronts as the question marker, 'gern' still closes the sentence.

go.habit.why: Plain present, time before place as in Standard German: the adverb sits between verb and destination. 'gaa' is irregular: ich gang.

go.prog.why: No progressive with a destination: the present plus 'jetzt grad' does the right-now work; 'am Gaa' exists but does not take a place phrase well.

go.past.why: Perfekt is the only past: 'bin' in second place, participle 'ggange' (doubled g) at the very end, everything else inside the bracket.

go.fut.why: Future is just present plus a time word: 'morn' is both 'will' and 'tomorrow'. 'wird' would sound like a guess or a promise.

go.neg.why: No auxiliary at all: 'nöd' follows the finite verb and precedes the destination.

live.now.why: Ongoing state is plain present plus 'sit' (for and since); no perfect. 'Jahr' stays singular after a number, and 'daa' closes the sentence.

live.past.why: Finished period goes Perfekt: 'ha' second, 'gwohnt' last, duration and place inside the bracket. 'lang' marks the span as closed.

live.fut.why: No future perfect: fronted 'Nächscht Jahr' forces inversion (wohne ich) and 'scho' (already) plus present does the 'will have lived' job.

live.q.why: Wh-word first, verb second (wohnsch du). The present carries the tense and 'scho' stands in for 'have been'.

if.real.why: 'wänn' is the spoken if; its clause is verb-final. The main clause inverts (gang ich) and 'travel' becomes 'gang go reise' with the doubled go.

if.unreal.why: Unreal condition uses the short subjunctive 'hett' at the end of the if-clause, then 'würd' plus infinitive; 'go' still slips in before reise.

if.past.why: Third conditional is participle plus 'hett' (gha hett). 'wär ich go reise' is the Perfekt of gaa without any participle: the go-construction drops ggange.
